common_name: Supertunia Black Satin Petunia (Glossy Near-Black Solid-Color Spreading Petunia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Black Satin's deep coloring shows best against pale companions like white Supertunia Vista Snowdrift or silvery foliage plants.

directions: Supertunia Black Satin produces glossy, velvety flowers in one of the deepest near-black purples available in the Supertunia line, a solid-color counterpart to the swirled Black Cherry and streaked Pretty Much Picasso introduced in the same Proven Winners series. Its mounding, moderately trailing habit is self-cleaning, dropping spent blooms cleanly without deadheading, and it holds its dark color well through summer heat rather than fading to a muddy brown-purple like many older near-black petunias. Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, fertilize regularly to keep the vigorous growth flowering, and pair with pale or silver-foliaged companions in containers to make the dramatic dark blooms stand out.

common_name: Wave Misty Lilac Petunia (Original Series Pale Lavender Spreading Groundcover Petunia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; like other original Wave series colors, Misty Lilac spreads low and wide as a flowering groundcover rather than mounding upright.

directions: Misty Lilac Wave carries soft, pale lavender-pink flowers with a faint darker throat, a gentler pastel alternative to the vivid magenta of the original Purple Wave that launched the series. It shares the same low, ground-hugging, rapidly spreading habit that made the Wave series famous, covering several feet of bed or trailing well over a container edge in a single season. Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, space generously to allow for its wide spread, and expect strong heat tolerance and largely self-cleaning blooms, with only an occasional midsummer shearing needed if growth becomes leggy.

common_name: Old Fashioned Vining Petunia (Fragrant Heirloom Trailing Petunia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained soil in full sun; this heirloom type is more openly vining than modern hybrid petunias and does best cascading from a hanging basket, window box, or tall container where its long trailing stems can hang freely.

directions: Old Fashioned Vining Petunia is a heirloom-type strain grown for its small, single violet-purple flowers and strong evening fragrance, traits closer to the wild Petunia integrifolia and Petunia axillaris species parents than to modern bred hybrids. Its stems trail and twine loosely rather than forming the dense mounded habit of modern spreading petunias, giving it a looser, old-cottage-garden look best suited to hanging baskets, window boxes, and tall urns where the vining stems can cascade freely. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, and because flowers are smaller and less self-cleaning than modern hybrids, deadhead lightly through the season to keep it tidy and blooming, especially valuable for the fragrance it releases in the evening near patios and porches.

common_name: Purple Pirouette Petunia (AAS-Winning Double Ruffled Purple-and-White Picotee Petunia)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost, since petunia seed is extremely fine and slow to reach transplant size; set out after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun.

directions: Purple Pirouette is an All-America Selections winning grandiflora petunia prized for its fully double, ruffled flowers in rich purple edged crisply in white, resembling a small ruffled rose or carnation more than a typical single-petaled petunia. Unlike the sprawling modern spreading series, it grows in a tidy, upright, well-branched mound that suits patio containers, window boxes, and border edging where its large, showy blooms can be appreciated up close. Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and deadhead regularly through the season, since the heavy double flowers do not self-clean as readily as modern single-flowered hybrids, to keep the plant blooming continuously from late spring through frost.
